questions.stem: Meridian Health, a 14-hospital system, has piloted Claude to draft discharge summaries from clinician notes. The sponsor now has to present results to the board and needs a defensible answer to "how do we know this is safe and better than what we do today?" Error analysis shows that about 62% of the note types in the pilot produce summaries a nurse would substantially rewrite, and the harm that matters most is in the medication list, where an anticoagulant gets dropped or mis-timed. Which approach defines success BEST?

options.text: Build a clinician-graded test set drawn from real discharge notes, score a harm-weighted error rate on the medication list alongside overall clinician-rated usefulness, and compare both against the same notes written the current way.
Cite the published benchmark results for the Claude model in use, which show it beats the previous model generation on summarization tasks, and translate that into a confidence claim for the board.
Rerun the drafting step on the most capable Claude tier with extended thinking, so the note types that produce rewrites improve and the board sees a better number.
Measure clinician minutes saved per discharge and present that as the headline metric, since it is the only measure the finance sponsor has ever agreed to fund.

questions.explanation: Translating a business problem into a Claude solution means deciding **what would have to be true for this to be worth deploying**, and then measuring exactly that. (A) does all three things an architect needs: a baseline (today's human-written summaries) so "better" has a referent, a labelled set drawn from the actual distribution rather than a convenient sample, and an error metric weighted toward the harm that actually occurs — medication-list errors, not a mean across all note types. The 62% rewrite rate is also an argument for measurement discipline, not for optimism: it says the pilot is not yet good, and the useful question is *which* note types and *which* errors. Anthropic's guidance on defining success is to write the criteria before tuning, and to measure against human performance on your own task rather than a general benchmark.

whyWrong.B: Public benchmarks describe performance on the benchmark's tasks and data. A hospital's abbreviations, its formulary and its medication-vocabulary risk are exactly what a benchmark cannot speak to — this is the most attractive distractor because a chart of benchmark deltas is easy to put in front of a board.
whyWrong.C: Moving to a larger model with extended thinking is a reasonable thing to *test*, and it may lift the difficult note types. But it changes cost and latency materially, and afterwards you still cannot say whether the medication harm is gone. It answers a question about model capability, not about whether this deployment is safe and better than the current process.
whyWrong.D: Clinician time is a legitimate efficiency measure and probably part of the value story, but on its own it is gameable — shorter summaries look faster and can be less useful — and it is blind to the medication failures that make the difference between a safe and an unsafe deployment.

questions.mindset: Define success as a measured comparison against today's baseline, weighted by the specific harm you are trying to remove.

questions.stem: The CFO of an industrial distributor opens the kickoff with: "I want AI to improve our product descriptions. They're bad, and sales say we lose deals on them. Can we have a demo by end of month?" Nothing else has been agreed. What is the architect's BEST first move?

options.text: Build a demo that rewrites the ten descriptions sales complains about most, using the most capable Claude tier, so the CFO sees something concrete and momentum carries into discovery.

Run structured discovery to turn the complaint into measurable requirements: which items and channels, what "good" looks like (there are 20 approved descriptions and a 30-page style guide), volume, who reviews, the accuracy bar, and what it costs today.
Settle the pattern now — this is bulk text generation, so build a fixed nightly workflow — because pattern choice has the largest effect on the schedule and the CFO needs a date.
Ask the CFO to choose between the three largest Claude models and a fine-tuned open model, so that the biggest line item in the budget is settled before anything else moves.

questions.explanation: A one-sentence business complaint is a hypothesis, not a specification. The first job is **structured discovery**, and this organisation happens to contain the definition of done: 20 approved descriptions and a style guide are both the rubric and a ready-made source of approved examples. Requirements have to be measurable before anything else is decided, because volume, latency tolerance, review model and cost per listing are precisely the inputs that determine pattern, model tier and deployment mode — the three things the distractors each pick at random.

whyWrong.A: Demos are good for expectation-setting, but a demo on ten cherry-picked items is evidence about those ten items, and it silently commits the project to the most expensive model tier. It also skips the discovery that would reveal whether the real catalogue is in scope and whether descriptions are even the constraint — the price, the images and the shipping terms may be what loses the deal.
whyWrong.C: Pattern selection is a *consequence* of requirements. Fixing it before knowing volume, latency tolerance and whether a human reviews each draft risks building an unattended nightly job for a workflow that turns out to need interactive editing and approval.
whyWrong.D: Model choice is downstream of requirements and of a baseline eval. Opening on it burns budget and creates a later migration, and a fine-tuned open model may not even be the comparison that matters for this task.

questions.mindset: A one-line business complaint is a hypothesis; turn it into measurable requirements before you commit to a pattern, a model or a demo.

questions.stem: An architecture group reviews six candidate automations for a regional grocery chain and concludes that two of them should not be built with a language model, whatever model is chosen. Which TWO candidates are those? Choose TWO.

options.text: Reconciling 40 store bank accounts against a fixed set of matching rules at month end, where the rules are documented and the exception path is already well understood.
Drafting a reply to a supplier who is disputing a promotion, grounded in an internal price-terms document set that is revised weekly.
Resizing and reformatting the supplier image assets that arrive each night so they match the catalogue system's required dimensions and format.
Generating a weekly personalised meal plan for each member from purchase history, declared dietary restrictions and the current in-store promotion calendar.
Archiving yesterday's price-export file to the compliance store under the filename convention the finance team specified.

questions.explanation: Part of translating a business problem is recognising when it is **not an LLM problem**. (A) is a documented rule set applied to structured records with a known exception path — deterministic reconciliation is faster, cheaper, reproducible and auditable, and a model adds variance to a task where the answer is a specific number. (E) is a file operation with a fixed naming convention; there is no judgement, ambiguity or natural-language understanding involved. (B) and (D) are the opposite shape: (B) requires reading changing terms and composing an argument that fits a specific dispute, and (D) requires balancing several soft constraints per member. Both are cases where the value comes precisely from tolerance of ambiguity that a rule set cannot encode.

whyWrong.B: Grounding a reply in a document set that changes weekly, in a way that has to answer this supplier's specific dispute, is retrieval plus judgement. The changing source is an argument for retrieval, not against a model — a fixed rules engine cannot compose that reply.
whyWrong.C: Resizing and reformatting images to a fixed spec is an image-processing task. There is no language understanding involved, so a model would add cost and variability for nothing.
whyWrong.D: Generating a plan from purchase history, declared restrictions and a live promotion calendar is generation over heterogeneous context with per-member trade-offs. The member count is a throughput and cost-planning problem, not a reason to avoid a model.

questions.mindset: Before choosing a pattern, ask whether the task needs model judgement at all — documented rules, fixed formats and file operations are better served deterministically.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical distributor's architecture group maintains a list of eleven candidate Claude use cases. The steering committee will fund exactly two this year and has set one hard constraint: each funded project must be able to show a measured improvement within one quarter. Which selection rule is the MOST defensible?

options.text: Rank by total annual hours the task consumes, fund the top two, and report the saving once each pilot is live.

Score each candidate on how measurable its current baseline is, how much genuine model judgement the task requires, whether the data and access already exist and are permitted, and the risk if the output is wrong — then fund the two with the strongest combination of a measurable baseline and real model advantage.
Fund the two whose executive sponsors are most senior, because senior sponsorship is the strongest predictor that a pilot survives contact with operations.
Fund the two that can be delivered as an autonomous agent, since agentic capability is what the market currently associates with AI leadership.

questions.explanation: Choosing between candidate use cases is a design decision, and the rule has to be defensible against the constraint that actually binds. (B) is: a measurable baseline means a before/after exists at all; genuine model judgement means the task is not a rule waiting to be written; existing, permitted data removes the most common month-one blocker; and error risk sizes the review effort. Crucially it is a *rule*, so the next funding round reuses it and the reasoning is auditable. Volume (A) is an input, not a screen — a 200,000-hour task with no baseline and no data access cannot demonstrate anything in a quarter. Sponsor seniority (C) predicts who will fight hardest, not what will work.

whyWrong.A: Hours consumed is a reasonable input but it is not sufficient on its own, and it actively misleads here: the largest task may have no measurable baseline and no permitted data, which makes it the *worst* candidate for a one-quarter proof.
whyWrong.C: Executive sponsorship is a delivery risk factor, not a value signal. Two projects selected this way can both stall on data access and consume the whole funding year without producing evidence of anything.
whyWrong.D: This is the modern-sounding selection rule that the constraint rules out. Agentic patterns are the most expensive to build, the hardest to evaluate deterministically and the slowest to prove value — they are the least likely candidates to demonstrate measured improvement inside a single quarter.

questions.mindset: Rank use cases by measurable baseline, genuine model advantage, data readiness and error risk — not by volume, sponsor rank or how modern the pattern sounds.

questions.stem: Kestrel Bank's internal assistant answers questions about the bank's own product terms from a document library. It scored 91% on the launch eval. Nine months later operations reports a rising complaint volume, and an audit shows the retrieval index has not been rebuilt since launch while the product team has revised terms three times. Engineers are arguing about whether the model or the prompt is at fault. What is the MOST architecturally sound response?

options.text: Treat this as a missing feedback loop rather than a model defect: rebuild the index on a schedule tied to document changes, add production sampling with human review, and fold newly labelled failures back into the eval set so it stops measuring September's system.
Move to the newest Claude model, on the basis that newer generations improve instruction-following and grounding in retrieved context, and re-measure afterwards.
Replace the frozen launch eval with a live benchmark that runs every night against the current model, so quality is always measured against today's capability.
Insert a second Claude call before answering that checks the drafted answer against the retrieved passages and rewrites it if they do not support it, so stale passages cannot produce wrong answers.

questions.explanation: This is a failure of the **feedback loop**, one of the four stages of an end-to-end Claude architecture: input, processing, output, and what flows back. The loop is missing in both directions — the index does not learn that documents changed, and production outcomes do not refresh the eval set — so quality silently diverges from what was measured. The correct architect's move is to close the loop and fix the input layer: rebuild the index when documents change, sample production traffic for human review, and refresh the labelled set so the eval reflects what customers actually ask. Note the discipline in "fold labelled failures back into the set": without labels the eval just measures itself.

whyWrong.B: A newer model cannot retrieve a document that is not in the index. Serving withdrawn product terms is an input-pipeline defect, and buying capability at the processing stage leaves customers confidently misinformed at greater cost.
whyWrong.C: A nightly live benchmark is the most attractive distractor because it sounds strictly more rigorous than a frozen eval. But measuring against the current model cannot attribute the failure: you will learn that quality fell without learning whether the cause is the index, the prompt, the model or the traffic mix — and a nightly job is a monitor, not a decision gate.
whyWrong.D: A verification pass is a legitimate mitigation for retrieved-passage noise and would reduce some confidently-wrong answers. It also doubles cost and latency on every request to work around a defect that a scheduled index rebuild removes for free.

questions.mindset: If quality decays after launch, suspect the feedback loop and the input layer before the model — an architecture with no path from production back into the system cannot notice drift.

questions.stem: Aldercroft University's course-enquiry assistant has thumbs-up and thumbs-down buttons wired to a spreadsheet, and the team intends to treat that as the feedback loop for improving the prompt. A colleague on the analytics team argues the loop will actively mislead them. Which TWO of her objections are correct? Choose TWO.

options.text: Raters are self-selected and their rate is low, so the rated population skews toward unusually happy or unusually angry cases and the mean rating is not an estimate of quality across all traffic.
Ratings arrive asynchronously, which makes them unusable as inputs to an online A/B test, since A/B tests require synchronous per-session feedback.
A rating is recorded per user rather than per query, so a question that was never rated cannot be counted at all and the denominator of the feedback metric is unknown.
Ratings are far too sparse to be worth collecting, so the loop should be dropped in favour of relying only on the thumbs-down cases, which at least represent real failures.

A rating measures whether an answer felt helpful, not whether it was factually correct, so the loop can be optimised for tone and fluency while groundedness errors persist unnoticed — correctness needs a graded labelled sample, not a rating.

questions.explanation: Both correct objections describe ways a rating-based loop breaks, and they break in different ways. (A) is **sampling bias**: non-response is both severe and non-random, so the mean rating among people who chose to rate is a biased estimate of quality across everyone — and the bias is not visible from the rating data alone. (E) is **construct validity**: a thumb measures perceived helpfulness, which a fluent, confident, wrong answer scores highly on. Together they mean the loop can be optimised to look good while remaining wrong. The fix is the same in both cases: keep ratings as a cheap signal, but add a proactive, stratified, human-graded sample of production traffic — including questions nobody rated — so you can compare the two populations and measure correctness directly.

whyWrong.B: Asynchronous feedback is a normal and useful input to online evaluation; it is also complementary to an offline eval set. The timing of a click has no bearing on whether the signal is usable.
whyWrong.C: The denominator is knowable — it is the set of queries for which a rating control was shown — and per-query recording is the normal design. This objection describes a hypothetical implementation flaw, not an inherent property of rating data.
whyWrong.D: Dropping ratings because the sample is sparse is worse than keeping them: thumbs-down is subject to the same self-selection bias, only from the negative side. The fix for sparse biased feedback is a proactive graded sample, not discarding the signal.

questions.mindset: Ratings measure feeling on a self-selected sample; correctness needs a proactive, stratified, human-graded sample of production traffic.

questions.stem: Northgate Insurance runs an adjuster assistant end to end: it ingests claim documents, extracts structured facts, retrieves coverage clauses, drafts a recommendation and writes back to the claims system. Six months after launch, adjusters say the drafts are "sounding right but missing the exception cases", and the vendor's own quality score is flat. The team proposes adding a self-review step where Claude critiques its own recommendation before it is written back. Which TWO arguments against that proposal are sound? Choose TWO.

options.text: The architecture has no trace of what the system retrieved or what it decided at each stage, so the team cannot tell whether the exception cases were lost in retrieval, in extraction, or in drafting — and adding a critic will not produce that information.

Exception handling is a policy decision that belongs to a human or a deterministic rules table, so a model critiquing its own output cannot resolve it; the case should be escalated with the retrieved clauses attached so a human can decide.
A self-critique step would break the existing downstream integration, because the claims system expects the recommendation in a fixed schema and a critique pass has no way to return to that schema.
Self-critique is known to degrade output quality on structured extraction tasks, so the pipeline would get worse even where it currently succeeds.

The recommendation stage already has a second opinion available in the pipeline: the coverage-clause retrieval step. Adding an unconstrained critic duplicates that without addressing the case where retrieval itself returned the wrong clause.

questions.explanation: Both correct arguments attack the proposal's premise rather than its cost. (A) is the strongest: the symptom — right-sounding answers that miss exceptions — is exactly the symptom of a pipeline with no per-stage observability. Without intermediate outputs you cannot attribute the failure to extraction, retrieval or drafting, and a self-critique only reads the final draft and the final retrieved clauses, so it inherits the same blind spot. (B) separates the two categories of failure hidden in one symptom: ordinary cases are a *pipeline quality* problem that tracing and per-stage evals fix, while genuine policy exceptions are a **governance boundary** and belong to a human or a rules table with the evidence attached. Escalation with the retrieved clauses is the design that makes the exception case an explicit, measurable path rather than an unstated failure.

whyWrong.C: A critic pass can be required to emit the same structured schema as the drafting step, or the critique can be a separate field the integration ignores. This is an implementation detail, not a reason the proposal is unsound.
whyWrong.D: Self-critique does not reliably degrade structured extraction, and the claim is not the issue anyway. Even if it were, the argument would be about tuning, not about why the architecture is failing.
whyWrong.E: Retrieval and self-critique are not substitutes. Retrieval returns what the clause store contains; a critique evaluates an answer. The claim that they overlap is the attractive-sounding rationale here, but it argues for removing the critic on cost grounds rather than on the grounds that neither fixes an unattributed failure.

questions.mindset: Before adding a model in front of a symptom, make the pipeline observable — and route genuine policy exceptions to humans rather than asking a model to adjudicate them.

questions.stem: An architect is documenting the end-to-end architecture of a recruitment assistant that screens CVs against a job description, writes interview questions and summarises interviewer notes. The team wants feedback loops in the design, and two engineers disagree about which parts qualify. Which TWO pieces of the design are genuine feedback loops? Choose TWO.

options.text: A weekly export of every candidate's stage, outcome and drop-off point into the analytics warehouse, so that the team can see where the funnel loses people.
The intake step that converts an uploaded PDF into plain text before it is sent to Claude.
A structured output schema that forces the screening step to return a score, a rationale and a list of evidence.
A prompt-caching breakpoint placed after the stable job-description block so the prefix is reused across candidates.
Recruiters record a reason whenever an interviewer rejects a candidate at any stage, and those reasons are reviewed monthly to revise the screening rubric and the questions the assistant generates.

questions.explanation: A feedback loop is output that **changes a future decision**: something produced downstream is routed back so the system adapts. (A) qualifies because stage and drop-off data from real candidates feeds back into how the funnel and the questions are designed and evaluated, and (E) qualifies because the human judgement recorded at the end of the pipeline — why a candidate was rejected — is fed back into the rubric and the generated questions, which is the strongest loop available because it carries ground truth. The other three are one-directional stages or implementation techniques: text extraction is an input transform, a structured schema is an interface contract on the output side, and prompt caching is a cost and latency optimisation on the input side. None of them causes anything upstream to be revised, which is precisely the distinction the architecture diagram has to get right.

whyWrong.B: PDF-to-text is the input stage. It transforms documents before the model sees them and produces nothing that flows back.
whyWrong.C: A structured schema shapes how one stage returns data. It improves reliability and testability, but the downstream fields never re-enter a prompt or a decision.
whyWrong.D: Prompt caching reuses an identical prefix across requests to cut input cost and time to first token. It is an input optimisation with no feedback path at all — a common mislabelling because it is technically part of the request.

questions.mindset: A feedback loop is output that changes a future decision; input transforms, output schemas and caching are not loops.

questions.stem: A furniture retailer's web chat fetches the current product catalogue and the store's delivery policy from its own API, then makes a single Claude call that answers the shopper's question and cites the products it used. The agent makes no tool calls, plans nothing, and runs in one request. Which pattern is this?

options.text: An augmented LLM — retrieval or external context is added to a single model call, with no autonomous planning or tool-use loop.
A prompt chain, because the product fetch and the delivery-policy fetch must happen before the answer is generated.
A routing workflow, because the system decides which data source to consult based on the shopper's question.
An agentic system, because the model decides at run time which products are relevant to the question.

questions.explanation: The defining features are all present: **external context is added to a single model call**, the data sources are chosen by application code rather than by the model, and there is no loop in which the model issues `tool_use` blocks and reacts to `tool_result`. That is the augmented-LLM pattern — the simplest form, and usually the right one when the task is "answer this question from these sources". Anthropic's guidance is to start here and add routing, chaining or agentic autonomy only when a specific limitation of the single call shows up in evals.

whyWrong.B: A prompt chain is a sequence of LLM calls where an earlier call's output feeds a later call's prompt, often with a gate in between. Fetching data from your own API is application code, not a model call, so there is one call here and no chain.
whyWrong.C: Routing means a classification step decides which downstream path handles the request — a separate specialised prompt, agent or flow per category. Nothing here classifies the shopper's question or dispatches it to a different handler.
whyWrong.D: Agentic means the model runs a loop, choosing and invoking tools itself and reacting to the results until it stops. Here the application decides what to fetch and the model answers once, so there is no agent loop.

questions.mindset: One model call plus retrieved context is an augmented LLM — start there and add routing, chaining or agentic autonomy only when a specific limitation shows up.

questions.stem: A bank's internal assistant must answer three kinds of question from three different knowledge areas: product terms, KYC obligations and complaint handling. Each area has its own approved document set, its own rules about what may be said to a customer, and its own reviewer. Today one large system prompt contains all three. Evals show the model blends rules from different areas. What is the MOST appropriate architectural change?

options.text: Split the knowledge areas into three dedicated retrieval indexes and add a classification step that routes each question to the matching area, so each area is served by its own scoped context and its own reviewer.
Give each area its own subagent and let the lead agent choose which subagent to call, so that context isolation is enforced by separate conversations rather than by routing logic.
Keep one index and one prompt but add XML section tags around each area's content and examples, so the model can see where each rule belongs.
Replace the single call with an evaluator-optimizer loop, so that a second call judges whether the answer stayed inside the correct knowledge area and rewrites it if not.

questions.explanation: The failure is **scope confusion between three domains that have genuinely different rules and different owners**. The cheapest correct fix is routing: classify the question, then serve it from the one scoped context that applies. That gives a small, auditable prompt per area, an index that can be permissioned and refreshed independently, and a reviewer per area — which is what the bank's stated constraint requires. Tagging (C) is the tempting cheap option and does help a model respect section boundaries, but it leaves one prompt holding all three rule sets and all three retrieval results, which is exactly where the blending happens, and it keeps every area's content in every request. A second call that judges and rewrites (D) adds cost and latency without ever having scoped the retrieval.

whyWrong.B: Subagents give context isolation, which sounds like the answer, but they are the heavier pattern and they do not solve the underlying problem on their own: a lead agent that chooses a subagent still has to classify correctly, and each subagent still needs its own scoped retrieval. Routing plus scoped indexes is the simpler mechanism for a fixed, enumerable set of knowledge areas.
whyWrong.C: Structural tags help a model attribute rules, and this is the option a sympathetic engineer defends. But every request still carries all three rule sets and all three retrieval results, so context grows and the opportunity for cross-contamination remains. It also keeps a single reviewer accountable for three rulebooks.
whyWrong.D: An evaluator-optimizer loop is for cases where quality is hard to specify in the prompt — writing, summarising, code. Here the problem is that the wrong context was in scope at all. Judging after the fact adds a second model call, doubles latency on every question, and cannot undo a confidently blended answer reliably.

questions.mindset: When a single prompt holds several rule sets with different owners, fix the scope with routing and per-area retrieval before you try to prompt the model to respect the boundaries.

questions.stem: A platform team is choosing among four candidate designs for four different internal features. Which TWO pairings are the BEST match of feature to pattern? Choose TWO.

options.text: A code-review agent that must decide for itself which files to open, run and revise, because the right steps depend on what it finds → an agentic loop with tools.

A nightly job that classifies 40,000 supplier invoices into 12 categories using a documented taxonomy, where results are needed by 8 a.m. and nobody waits → a fixed batch workflow with a single classifier step.

An assistant that writes product descriptions in a fixed brand voice from an approved style guide, where the inputs are known and the format is fixed → routing to five specialised agents, one per product category.

A research assistant answering "compare the three shortlisted vendors on security posture" by reading each vendor's security pack in turn → parallelization with one subagent per vendor, fanned out by the application.

A drafting assistant for settlement letters that must not invent clause numbers, where a wrong clause number has legal consequences → an evaluator-optimizer loop that rewrites until a judge model approves.

questions.explanation: (A) is the genuine agentic case: **the steps cannot be known before the work starts**, which is the condition that justifies letting a model choose its own tool calls. (D) is the genuine parallelization case: the three vendors are **independent**, so fanning them out concurrently and aggregating is both faster and cheaper than reading them in sequence. (B) and (C) are the modern-sounding answers that are wrong for the same underlying reason — they add structure where none is needed. (B) is a single classification over a documented taxonomy: no planning, no dependency, no judgement about approach, and the wait time is zero, so a batch workflow with one step is the whole answer. (C) is a single generation task with known inputs and a fixed format; five agents add routing latency and five prompts to maintain, and gain nothing. (E) is the governance-skipping anti-pattern: where a wrong clause number has legal consequences, a judge model that "approves" is not a verification step, because it cannot check the clause exists in the source document. That check belongs in code against the clause store, with human review on exceptions.

whyWrong.B: Classification against a documented taxonomy is one model call with a schema. There is nothing to plan, nothing to parallelise and no run-time decision, so a full agent or a routing tree is pure overhead — and overhead on 40,000 items a night is a real number.
whyWrong.C: Writing from an approved style guide with known inputs is a single generation step. Category-based routing implies the category changes what must be done; here it only changes a few words, so five agents and five prompts buy nothing and add five places to keep consistent.
whyWrong.E: An LLM judge cannot verify that a clause number exists in the source contract; it can only assess whether the answer looks plausible. For a legal consequence, the verification must be a deterministic check against the clause store plus human review of exceptions — the "most automated" option here is exactly the one that skips the step that would catch the error.

questions.mindset: Agentic when steps cannot be predicted, parallel when subtasks are independent, fixed workflow when neither applies — and never let a model judge substitute for a deterministic check where an error has consequences.

questions.stem: A marketing team wants Claude to write 6,000 product-page descriptions in a fixed house style from a template with a known set of fields. They have prototyped it as an autonomous agent with three subagents — one plans the page structure, one writes copy, one checks style compliance and rewrites until it passes. The prototype takes about 90 seconds and $0.40 per page. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Replace it with a fixed pipeline: fill the template deterministically from the fields, make one Claude call per page to write the copy, validate the output against the style guide in code, and retry only the failed validation cases.
Keep the agent but remove the style-checking subagent, since style compliance is better handled by giving the writer subagent the full 30-page style guide in its system prompt.
Keep all three subagents but run them on the cheaper fast model tier and batch the work overnight, which preserves the architecture while bringing cost within budget.
Keep the structure but merge the plan and write stages into a single subagent, so that planning overhead is removed while the compliance check stays independent.

questions.explanation: Every precondition for an agentic pattern is absent here: the inputs are **known and structured** (a template with a fixed field set), the output shape is **fixed**, the compliance criteria are **documented and checkable**, and there is **no run-time decision**. So this is a fixed pipeline with one generation step, and the style check belongs in code where it is deterministic, cheap and auditable — retrying only failures rather than paying for a judge on every page. At 6,000 pages the economics are decisive: $0.40 a page is $2,400 a run, and a 90-second agentic run means the whole job takes a day of wall-clock orchestration. Note the trap in the alternatives: they all keep the agentic architecture and tune it, which never addresses the root cause.

whyWrong.B: Moving the compliance burden into the writer's prompt is the opposite of verification — it asks the same system to both produce the copy and certify it, and it puts 30 pages of style guide into every request. It also removes the only stage that was producing an objective signal.
whyWrong.C: Moving to a cheaper tier and the Batches API is real cost engineering and may be part of the answer, but it leaves a three-agent architecture in place for a task that needs none of the three agents. It optimises the wrong layer.
whyWrong.D: Merging the planner and writer removes one subagent, which is an improvement, but it retains agentic orchestration — including the writer and the compliance checker — where the task is fully specified. The style check should become a deterministic validation, not another model that approves.

questions.mindset: If the inputs, the output shape and the check are all known in advance, build a fixed pipeline with code-side validation — not an agent with a self-approving critic.

questions.stem: A due-diligence platform reviews one acquisition target per deal. The lead agent must produce a 40-page report covering financial performance, legal exposure, customer concentration, competitive position and management quality. Each section needs deep reading of hundreds of pages, and the whole source corpus is about 900,000 tokens. Evals show the single-agent version produces shallow sections because the report-writing stage is competing with the reading for context. What is the BEST architectural change?

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: the lead agent plans the section list, dispatches one subagent per section with that section's scope and its own isolated context, then writes the report from the structured findings the subagents return.
Orchestrator-workers, but have each subagent write its section as finished prose and pass the prose to the lead agent, so the lead can assemble the report without re-reading any source.
Increase the context window available to the single agent by moving the corpus to a retrieval index, so every section has access to all relevant pages at once.
Split the target's business into five independent Claude calls, one per section, and concatenate their prose output into the report without a lead agent.

questions.explanation: This is the textbook case for **orchestrator-workers with context isolation**: the work decomposes into five roughly independent sections, each large enough to overflow a shared context, and the coordinator only needs a synthesis of findings rather than the source material. Anthropic's multi-agent research write-up makes the same argument: subagents work in their own context windows, so each can dig deep, and the lead agent's context stays proportional to the number of findings rather than the size of the corpus. The subagent return contract matters as much as the fan-out — structured findings with citations keep the synthesis stage verifiable, and they give you per-section evals for free.

whyWrong.B: Returning finished prose is the tempting variant because it saves a synthesis step. It removes the evidence trail: the lead agent cannot check a claim against the source section, per-section quality becomes unmeasurable, and one weak subagent's confident prose is indistinguishable from a strong one at the point of assembly.
whyWrong.C: Retrieval fixes a context-size problem, not an attention-allocation problem. With one agent still writing all five sections, the reading and writing of section four still compete for the same window, and the shallow-sections symptom persists. It also re-adds 900,000 tokens of retrieval churn to every run.
whyWrong.D: Five calls with no coordinator drops the section plan, drops any cross-section consistency (management quality in the legal section versus in the competitive section) and produces no gate when one section fails. Concatenation is not synthesis, and there is nowhere to record that one of the five came back incomplete.

questions.mindset: When one agent's reading and writing compete for the same context, give each unit of work its own window and return structured findings to a coordinator.

questions.stem: A healthcare provider's clinical-notes agent uses a lead agent that dispatches three subagents: a summariser, a medication-extraction agent and a guidelines lookup agent. Each subagent has its own context, which is why the team chose this design. In production, the medication list in the final note is wrong about 9% of the time, and the failure rate is highest on patients with five or more medications. The lead agent's own logs show it received the subagents' outputs and assembled the note correctly. Which explanation does the architect take seriously?

options.text: The failure is at the interface: subagents returned free-text summaries, and the lead agent reassembled them into a list it never re-derived from source, so it could not detect a medication that a subagent dropped. The fix is a structured, itemised medication contract with source references, validated for completeness before assembly.

The failure is the model tier. Move all three subagents and the lead to the most capable Claude tier, since medication reconciliation with five or more items requires deeper reasoning than the current tier provides.
The failure is that there are three subagents rather than one, and consolidating into a single agent with all three tools would restore the cross-checking that isolation removed.

The failure is a missing extended-thinking step on the assembly call, because assembling a medication list from three summaries is exactly the kind of task that benefits from explicit reasoning about completeness.

questions.explanation: The diagnostic clue is that the lead agent's logs show correct assembly — so the error entered **upstream of assembly**, in what the subagents returned. Multi-agent designs move work into subagents and hand back a summary; if that return value is prose, the lead agent has no way to tell a complete list from a lossy one, and there is no verification step at the boundary. That is an interface-design failure, and the fix is to make the contract structured and itemised with source references, plus a completeness check (for example, that the count of extracted medications matches the count the extractor claims to have seen) before the note is assembled. It scales with the failure pattern: errors grow with list length because each item is another chance for a lossy summary.

whyWrong.B: A larger model is the reflex answer and it is not free of merit — but the logs already tell you the lead agent assembled what it was given correctly. Raising the tier everywhere raises cost and latency on every note in exchange for a guess about a stage the evidence does not implicate, and it leaves the lossy interface exactly as it is.
whyWrong.C: Collapsing to one agent does restore shared context and cross-checking, and for a task this small (three subagents, one patient note) it is arguably the right architecture anyway. But that is an argument for simplifying the design, not a diagnosis: the same lossy-prose problem appears in single-agent chains, and it does not explain why the rate climbs with medication count.
whyWrong.D: Extended thinking on the assembly call is a plausible-sounding mitigation and would be a reasonable experiment. It cannot work here, though: the information needed to notice a missing medication is not in the lead agent's context. Reasoning harder over an incomplete summary cannot recover an item that was never passed along.

questions.mindset: When a multi-agent pipeline produces wrong output, check whether the boundary contract lets the coordinator detect a lossy handoff before you reach for a bigger model.

questions.stem: In an Agent SDK implementation, a lead agent must obtain four independent pieces of information — the customer's last 12 months of transactions, their open support tickets, their shipping history and their account tier — from four separate MCP tools, then write one summary. No tool depends on another's output. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Have the lead agent issue all four `tool_use` blocks in a single assistant message so they execute in parallel, then summarise the four `tool_result` blocks.
Create four subagents, one per data source, and let the lead agent collect their answers sequentially before summarising.
Wrap all four data sources behind a single aggregate MCP tool so the lead agent makes one tool call instead of four.
Have the lead agent call the four tools in four separate turns so that each `tool_result` can be checked against the others before the next call is made.

questions.explanation: Independent tool calls should be issued **in the same assistant message**, and the API executes them in the same block — all `tool_result` blocks come back in a single following user message. That is one model turn instead of eight, which directly reduces latency and cost without any orchestration machinery. Subagents (B) would add four context windows and four model lifecycles to gather four values. Aggregating into one tool (C) hides the structure and creates a bespoke endpoint for every combination of question. Serialising into four turns (D) is the tempting conservative choice — ‘check each result before the next’ — but it cannot check anything, because at turn two the agent has nothing to check against.

whyWrong.B: Four subagents for four independent lookups is the heavy pattern — four contexts, four tool loops and four model lifecycles — applied to the easiest possible task. Anthropic's guidance is that subagents are for tasks that need their own context window, not for fanning out trivial reads.
whyWrong.C: An aggregate tool would work, but it means maintaining a bespoke endpoint per question shape, and it hides the individual results behind one opaque payload, which makes per-tool tracing and per-tool evals harder. It solves a problem that parallel tool calls already solve.
whyWrong.D: Serialising is not a check. With no cross-check possible at turn two, the extra turns only add latency. If genuine cross-validation is wanted, it should be an explicit step that sees all four results, not an artefact of ordering them.

questions.mindset: Independent lookups belong in one assistant message as parallel tool_use blocks; subagents are for work that needs its own context window.

questions.stem: A legal-tech firm runs a contract-review agent that fans out one subagent per contract clause type across 80 contracts. Runs take 40 minutes, cost about $14 each, and about 1 run in 30 produces a report that a reviewer describes as 'confidently wrong on the penalty clauses'. The firm wants to standardise multi-agent orchestration across all its products. Which TWO changes give the MOST value? Choose TWO.

options.text: Give every run a hard wall-clock and token budget, and make the lead agent write a partial, clearly-marked report when it hits the budget rather than continuing or failing the whole job.

Require each subagent to return structured findings with the clause number and a verbatim quote from the source for every assertion, and have the lead agent cite them in the report so a reviewer can check each claim in seconds.
Move the fan-out to run every clause type against every contract in a single batch, so the whole job is one request and the cost becomes predictable from the contract count.
Add a verifier subagent at the end of the run whose job is to check the assembled report against the source contracts and rewrite any section it cannot support.
Standardise on a single Claude model tier for every subagent and every product, so that behaviour, cost and eval results are comparable across the portfolio.

questions.explanation: (B) and (A) are the two changes that address the two real failure modes of long multi-agent runs. (B) attacks **unverifiability**: the reason a reviewer can call a report ‘confidently wrong’ is that nothing in the pipeline connects a claim to the clause it came from, so verification is a re-read of 80 contracts. Structured findings with clause references and verbatim quotes make the report auditable by construction and give you per-clause-type evals. (A) attacks **unbounded duration**: 40-minute, $14 runs with no budget mean a single slow subagent either stalls everything or silently produces an incomplete report; an explicit budget plus a marked-partial output converts a failure into a visible, reviewable state. The modern-sounding options are exactly the ones to resist: (D) adds a verifier model that re-reads the corpus to check the corpus — expensive, no better than citing the source — and (C) trades a per-clause context for one enormous request whose context no single call can hold.

whyWrong.C: Batching makes cost arithmetically predictable but destroys the isolation that made subagents useful: one request covering 80 contracts by 8 clause types cannot hold the source material, and a single failure contaminates everything in the batch. Predictable cost on an architecture that no longer fits the task is not a win.
whyWrong.D: A verifier subagent re-reading the sources is the appealing fully-automated answer. It roughly doubles cost, adds another 20 minutes of latency, and — critically — a model checking a model is a second opinion, not a verification: if the verifier's reading of the penalty clause is wrong too, nothing catches it. Citing the source clause puts the check in front of a human reviewer, who can do it in seconds.
whyWrong.E: Standardising the model tier across the portfolio helps cost predictability and comparability, but it is a governance and procurement decision, not a fix for either failure mode. Forcing every product onto one tier would push a clause-extraction subagent and a synthesis subagent to the same setting, which is a capability compromise with no offsetting benefit here.

questions.mindset: Standardise multi-agent orchestration around budgets and auditable handoffs — not around more agents, and never around a model verifying another model.

questions.stem: A manufacturer wants Claude to standardise quality reporting across 12 plants. Each plant's engineers describe their own format; the target is one report structure with the same nine sections everywhere, produced monthly. The obvious decomposition is one Claude call per plant per month, run in parallel. Which factor should MOST change that decomposition?

options.text: Whether the nine sections can be produced by a single call per plant, or whether the data for some sections must be fetched with tools first — because a step that needs tool calls needs its own turn and its own place in the plan.
Whether the plants run in the same time zone, because report generation deadlines are stated in local time.
Whether the nine section names are the same at every plant, because different headings would require a different prompt.
Whether the engineers at each plant are Claude Code users, because that affects how the prompts are distributed.

questions.explanation: Decomposition should follow the shape of the work, and the question “does this step need tool calls?” is the one that changes the shape of a Claude pipeline. A step that must fetch plant data from a MES before writing needs its own tool-use turns, so it cannot be the same single call as the writing step — it becomes a fetch stage followed by a synthesis stage, each separately evaluable. This is exactly the reason to decompose by *capability needed* rather than by *unit of output*: it produces boundaries where you can log, evaluate and retry independently. Parallelising across plants remains correct, because the plants are independent of each other.

whyWrong.B: Time zones affect scheduling of the run, not the decomposition of the work. A monthly report per plant has the same internal structure whatever clock it runs on, and a scheduler can handle the offsets.
whyWrong.C: Non-uniform headings are a prompt-content problem, solvable with a canonical section list in the prompt. The premise also says the target is one report structure everywhere, which is the point of the project.
whyWrong.D: How the prompt reaches the plant has nothing to do with how the report is broken into steps. It is a distribution and rollout concern.

questions.mindset: Decompose by the capability each step needs — does it call tools, or is it a single generation — not by the shape of the final document.

questions.stem: A university's admissions team runs an application-screening assistant over 40,000 applications. The decomposition is: extract the transcript, extract the personal statement, score each against the rubric, then write a decision summary. Screening quality is the metric that matters and it is slipping. Which change to the decomposition is MOST likely to help?

options.text: Score each extracted element with its own rubric-graded step that returns a score plus the specific evidence for it, then have the final summary combine those scores — so a scoring failure can be attributed to an element rather than to the application as a whole.
Merge extraction and scoring into one call per application, so the model sees the transcript and the rubric at the same time while it decides the score.
Split scoring across three parallel calls — academic, extracurricular, personal — and average them, so that no single rubric dimension dominates the outcome.
Add a final Claude call that re-reads the whole application and rewrites the decision summary if it disagrees with the element scores.

questions.explanation: When a pipeline's end metric slips, decomposition earns its keep by making **each step separately evaluable**. (A) does that: element-level scores each carry their own evidence, so a labelled set can tell you whether the transcript extraction, the statement extraction or the scoring step is where quality is lost — and a 40,000-application pipeline needs that attribution to avoid re-tuning the wrong stage. It also gives admissions a per-element audit trail, which they will need regardless. Merging (B) makes attribution impossible, averaging (C) hides disagreement rather than diagnosing it, and a final rewriting call (D) acts on a symptom three steps downstream.

whyWrong.B: Putting extraction and scoring in one call is defensible on latency grounds and loses nothing in principle — but it destroys the ability to evaluate the two stages apart, which is the specific thing this team needs now that a composite metric is slipping. When a metric fails and you cannot attribute it, merging is the wrong direction.
whyWrong.C: Averaging three rubric dimensions hides a real signal: if one dimension is being scored wrongly, averaging dilutes it rather than surfacing it. And it does not establish ground truth — it only adds structure. Per-element evaluation with evidence is what makes the failure locatable.
whyWrong.D: A summariser that rewrites when it disagrees with the element scores is a symptom-level patch. It adds a full extra pass over 40,000 applications, and the rewritten summary would then have no rubric of its own to be checked against.

questions.mindset: When a composite metric slips, make each step separately evaluable before you merge steps or add another pass.

questions.stem: A property management company processes 12,000 lease documents a month. Each lease must produce: a structured set of key terms (dates, rent, break clauses), a risk flag if any non-standard clause is present, and a one-paragraph summary. Which decomposition is the most defensible starting point?

options.text: Three steps per document — extract terms into a fixed schema, check the extracted terms against the non-standard clause rules in code, then write the summary from the verified terms.
One step per document — a single call reads the lease and returns terms, flags and summary together, because three calls per lease triples cost across 12,000 leases.
Two steps — a first call extracts terms and flags risk, and a second independent call reads the raw lease again and writes the summary, so the summary is not biased by the extraction.
One agent per document that is given a `read_lease` tool and a `check_clause` tool, and is instructed to complete all three outputs before stopping.

questions.explanation: The decomposition should follow the reliability of each sub-task. Term extraction into a fixed schema is exactly what structured outputs do well. Clause comparison against **known, documented rules** is deterministic and belongs in code — putting it in a prompt means asking a model to apply a rulebook, which is where non-standard-clause detection drifts. The summary is the only genuinely generative step, and it should be written from the verified terms so it cannot contradict them. This is also the decomposition that keeps cost low: 12,000 documents x three small calls is far cheaper than 12,000 long-context single calls, because the second and third calls work on extracted terms rather than the full lease.

whyWrong.B: Cost is being miscounted. A single call must carry the whole lease in context to do all three jobs, whereas the three-step version carries the full lease once and then works with a few hundred tokens of extracted terms twice — so it is both cheaper and more testable. Merging is a false economy.
whyWrong.C: Having the summary written independently from the raw lease sounds like a useful independence check, but it produces summaries that can contradict the extracted terms — and the extracted terms are the record of truth. Double-reading the lease is also the single largest cost item in the pipeline.
whyWrong.D: An agent with two tools is the flexible answer, and it is heavier than needed for a fixed three-output task. It also puts the clause check inside the model's discretion, where non-standard clauses will eventually be missed, and it makes the outputs harder to validate because they arrive interleaved with tool calls.

questions.mindset: Decompose by the reliability of each sub-task: model the fuzzy generation, and give the rulebook and the arithmetic to code.

questions.stem: A public-sector agency's citizen assistant must answer benefit questions. The agency's director wants a single headline figure to take to the treasury: “it saves 12 full-time equivalents.” Which measurement design BEST supports that claim?

options.text: Measure end-to-end handling time per citizen contact before and after, on the same contact mix, and convert the delta into staff hours only where the assistant genuinely removed the work — with contacts it merely deflected counted as a separate line.
Count the number of citizen contacts handled by the assistant per month, since handling volume is the clearest single proxy for capacity released.
Ask caseworkers to rate how much of their workload the assistant takes off them each week, on a five-point scale, and report the mean rating as a percentage of their time.
Report total contacts served per adviser per day before and after, on the assumption that the ratio is stable across roles.

questions.explanation: A headcount-equivalent claim has to be derived from **the work actually removed**, measured on the same contact mix, with deflection handled explicitly. (A) is the honest accounting: it holds the input mix constant so the comparison is like-for-like, and it separates the two effects that a single FTE number hides — contacts the assistant resolved outright, and contacts it deflected (which usually shift rather than disappear, and can land on the phone channel). Deflection is where transformation-pillar claims usually overstate the productivity pillar. The correct output is often two numbers, not one, and that is a more defensible thing to take to a treasury than a headline.

whyWrong.B: Contacts handled is a throughput metric, not a time-saved metric. A contact that the assistant answers in twenty seconds and a contact it handles badly in eight minutes both count as one, so volume tells you nothing about capacity released — and it silently includes deflection.
whyWrong.C: Self-reported workload reduction is the metric most vulnerable to optimism, and asking workers to convert a feeling into a percentage guarantees one. It is not a measurement of the work; it is a measurement of the story people tell about the work.
whyWrong.D: Contacts per adviser conflates the assistant's effect with every other change in the period — staffing, seasonality, channel mix — and holds adviser roles equivalent when casework varies enormously by complexity. It cannot be audited back to a time basis.

questions.mindset: A headcount-equivalent claim must come from measured work removed on a like-for-like mix, with deflection counted separately.

questions.stem: An insurance group is choosing between two configurations for its claims-drafting assistant. Config X uses a mid-tier model with prompt caching on the stable policy block and reports 97.4% agreement with human-written drafts at $0.11 per claim, p95 2.1 seconds. Config Y uses the top-tier model with no caching at 98.9% agreement, $0.38 per claim, p95 5.4 seconds. The claims director says the 1.5-point agreement difference is what matters; finance says cost and latency make X the only viable option at 90,000 claims a month. What does the architect do?

options.text: Establish whether the 1.5 points of disagreement are concentrated in the claims that actually cost money — if they are spread evenly across routine low-value claims, X with human review on flagged cases is the defensible choice, and if they concentrate in high-severity claims, X needs routing so those go to Y.
Choose X, because at 90,000 claims a month the saving is about $24,000 a month and latency compliance matters more than 1.5 points of agreement.
Choose Y, because agreement with human drafts is the closest available proxy for draft quality, and the cost difference is affordable at this volume.
Deploy both and average their outputs, which is a standard technique for reducing the variance between two model configurations.

questions.explanation: This is a genuine trade-off, so the architect's job is to find out **which axis the disagreement lies on** rather than to pick a side on instinct. Aggregate agreement is a poor decision metric because it weights a routine low-value claim the same as a contested injury claim worth five figures. Error analysis on the labelled disagreements tells you which configuration you actually need and where; a routing design that sends only the severe or low-confidence cases to Y gets most of Y's agreement at close to X's unit cost, which satisfies both the director and finance. That is the answer that respects both constraints rather than declaring one of them wrong. (B) and (C) are both single-criterion decisions dressed up as judgements, and (D) is not a real technique — averaging two independent model outputs produces a third answer that is not more correct, just different, and it doubles the cost.

whyWrong.B: This decides on unit economics alone and assumes 1.5 points is small without checking where the disagreements are. If the disagreements concentrate in high-severity claims — exactly the claims where a wrong draft generates a complaint or a regulatory issue — then the saving is being funded by an increase in review workload and risk downstream. Finance's number is real; it is not the whole decision.
whyWrong.C: This decides on a single quality proxy alone, and the proxy is questionable: agreement with human drafts is not the same as quality, since a human draft can itself be poor. It also ignores that a 5.4-second p95 may breach an adjuster's workflow SLA, which turns a cost decision into a process failure.
whyWrong.D: There is no established technique of averaging the outputs of two differently-configured model calls and gaining quality from it. Two independent generations are not two noisy estimates of one answer — they may disagree substantively — so the average is an unvalidated third answer, produced at roughly double the cost, with no way to attribute its quality.

questions.mindset: When two configurations disagree, find out where the disagreements are before choosing — then route the expensive model only to the cases that need it.

questions.stem: A logistics company moves 45,000 freight-invoice documents a week through Claude for field extraction. Contracts with shippers require results within one business day; internal analysts want cost per document below $0.30; and the finance team wants field-level accuracy at or above 99%. What design does the architect recommend?

options.text: Run the extraction as a batch workload on the Message Batches API, use a mid-tier model with a strict schema, validate the JSON in code and route the small percentage that fails validation to a more capable model with human review — then measure all three criteria on a labelled sample before launch.

Run the extraction synchronously on the top-tier model so that every document gets the highest accuracy, and rely on prompt caching on the shared freight-invoice instructions to bring cost under $0.30.
Run the extraction synchronously on a mid-tier model, since synchronous calls return immediately and the one-business-day contract is comfortably met by any configuration.
Run the extraction as a batch workload on a small fast model, and send the 2% of documents whose validation fails to a human to complete manually, so no model is asked to handle a document twice.

questions.explanation: All three constraints are satisfiable at once and the design has to satisfy them **jointly**. The one-business-day deadline means nobody is waiting, which is the textbook condition for the **Message Batches API** — a materially cheaper path for bulk work. A mid-tier model plus a strict schema and code-side JSON validation protects the 99% accuracy floor cheaply, and routing the validation failures to a more capable model buys back most of the remaining accuracy without paying for it on every document. The final clause is the architect's discipline: state the three criteria, then measure them on a labelled sample before committing, because these are exactly the numbers that will be quoted back in a quarter. (B) spends to hit the accuracy target where it is already met and misuses caching — caching reuses an identical prefix, it does not make an expensive model cheap. (C) misreads the SLA as though synchronous were automatically correct, when the binding constraint here is throughput and cost, not latency. (D) sends failures to a person rather than a model, which quietly converts a model-accuracy problem into a staffing cost the company has not budgeted.

whyWrong.B: Top-tier on every document is buying accuracy that the schema plus validation already delivers for most of them, at roughly the cost the finance team ruled out. Prompt caching does not rescue it either: caching cuts the cost of a repeated prefix, so it helps a shared-instructions design and does nothing to reduce the cost of the tokens actually being generated per document.
whyWrong.C: Synchronous is the wrong mode when nobody waits and the deadline is a full business day. It is not wrong as a latency strategy — it is wrong as a cost and throughput strategy here, and it leaves the batch discount on the table for 45,000 documents a week.
whyWrong.D: Routing failures to a human avoids paying a model twice, but it does not address the accuracy target — it re-labels a model limitation as a manual workload. Nobody in the scenario has agreed to staff manual completion for roughly 900 documents a week, which is the kind of hidden cost an architect should surface rather than assume.

questions.mindset: When nobody is waiting, use batch; protect the accuracy floor with schema validation and route only the failures to a stronger model.
